content: The average cost of treatments provided was approximately USD 124 per treatment, regardless of their effectiveness. At that time, the most effective product available cost USD 640 per treatment, but the manufacturer could only supply 1,250 treatments, making this cost unsustainable for large-scale distribution. In comparison, the cost of treatment for other neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) is significantly lower. For instance, post-exposure prophylaxis for rabies costs as little as USD 12 per treatment. Convincing countries and donors to accept the much higher costs of antivenoms is challenging, and ensuring the necessary supply will require substantial market growth and increased industrial production. Improved access to academic research outcomes, new technologies, and technical assistance can help manufacturers reduce unnecessary costs, streamline and modernize production, and deliver products at more affordable prices. Snakebite envenoming is preventable. The risk of snakebite envenoming can be reduced through community education and measures that often overlap with the prevention of other diseases. For example, using bed nets to prevent mosquito-borne diseases can also reduce the risk of snakebites from snakes entering homes at night. Encouraging individuals to protect their feet, ankles, and lower legs by wearing boots not only protects them from snakebites but also from infections caused by soil-transmitted helminths, bacteria, fungi, podoconiosis, and trauma associated with walking or working barefoot. Snakebite envenoming is treatable. Effective means for treating snakebite envenoming are available, and ensuring that those bitten have access to safe, effective, and affordable medicines can significantly reduce the mortality and disability caused by snakebites. Technological support, investment, and training can rapidly improve the production and regulation of antivenoms. This will not only enhance snakebite treatment but also improve the safety and quality of other biotherapeutics, such as those for diphtheria, tetanus, and rabies, as well as other drugs and equipment necessary to treat infections and organ failures. Empowered communities with well-functioning health systems that have access to safe and effective medicines can effectively prevent and control snakebite envenoming. When communities recognize the value of prevention, risk avoidance, and early medical care for snakebite envenoming, outcomes improve. More individuals will seek help sooner, suffer less, and have a higher likelihood of survival and recovery. Community education to promote better health-seeking behavior and injury prevention, training of health workers, stronger health systems, and access to high-quality medicines will benefit everyone and contribute to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Teaching health professionals fundamental clinical skills not only improves their ability to diagnose and treat snakebite envenoming but also enhances their overall medical practice. Similarly, improvements in health systems for managing snakebites benefit the broader health needs of the population. Snakebite envenoming is a multi-organ system disease that requires holistic management and expertise across various medical disciplines. Better access to medicines, training, and provision of basic equipment and laboratory services will increase the return on investment and bring some of the most vulnerable populations closer to universal health coverage. Investment in the prevention and treatment of snakebite envenoming saves victims from poverty and reduces health inequity. Most victims of snakebite envenoming live in impoverished, vulnerable communities with poor health indicators, often in rural areas of tropical and subtropical regions in Africa, the Middle East, Asia, Oceania, and Latin America. A venomous snakebite can lead to death or prolonged periods of depression, disability, and economic destitution. Without access to effective treatment, many victims lose their livelihoods, savings, and property. A debilitating snakebite may render an agricultural worker unable to work, forcing them to rely on family support. The economic consequences, marginalization, and stigmatization often extend to their immediate and extended families. Investment in antivenoms can alleviate the suffering of victims and their families, giving them a chance to recover, rebuild their lives, and resume their roles as productive members of their communities. Investment in improving snakebite prevention and controlling its incidence is part of achieving SDG 1, which aims to end poverty in all its forms, and aligns with the commitment of Member States to leave no one behind. It also supports SDG 3, which seeks to achieve universal health coverage and access to safe, effective, quality, and affordable essential medicines and vaccines for all. The World Health Organization (WHO) has based its 13th Global Programme of Work on a commitment to leave no one behind. The right to the highest attainable standard of health, as expressed in WHO’s Constitution, underpins all of WHO’s work. WHO is committed to gender equality, equity, and rights-based approaches to health to enhance participation, build resilience, and empower communities. Investment in antivenoms will fulfill these commitments and WHO’s goals of ensuring that one billion more people have health coverage, one billion more lives are made safer, and one billion more lives are improved. It will accelerate progress toward achieving universal health coverage by 2030, creating a safer, healthier, and fairer world where all individuals can live productive, fulfilling, and active lives. The prevention and treatment of snakebite envenoming is a model of collaboration for the One Health approach. Snakebite envenoming also causes substantial economic losses by disabling and killing livestock and working animals. Engaging with communities to prevent human snakebites may increase their awareness of the often-overlooked problem of fatal and debilitating snakebites among valuable domestic livestock. Coordination between human and veterinary health systems to reduce the impact of snakebite envenoming on communities serves as a model for other One Health collaborations. The strategy for snakebite envenoming prevention and control includes ensuring safe, effective treatment, empowering and engaging communities, strengthening health systems, and increasing partnerships, coordination, and resources. The implementation will occur in three phases: a pilot phase (2019–2020) in 10–12 high-burden countries, a scale-up phase (2021–2024) extending to 35–40 countries, and a full roll-out phase (2025–2030) to all affected countries. The goal is to halve the number of deaths and cases of disability caused by snakebite envenoming by 2030.
